title: Down the Nile in Chains
sum: The king's letter goes out, and the book shows what it did. In the towns the Gentiles hold public feasts while the Jews mourn. Old men, brides and young husbands are chained and shipped down the Nile in the dark, landed at Schedia and penned in the hippodrome outside Alexandria. When Jews of the city slip out to mourn them, the king orders that they be treated the same way.

Then the king orders every Jew in Egypt registered by name, so that all may be killed in a single day. For forty days the clerks work from dawn to dusk while the king feasts before his idols. At last they report that they cannot finish: there are too many Jews, and the papyrus and the pens have run out. It was "the unconquerable providence of him who helped the Jews from heaven" (4:21).
readings: Historians find a real world under the story: Nile boats, the toll port of Schedia (Strabo, Geography 17.1.16), a racecourse outside the walls, and the registers of Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt. The forced deportation of a whole people and a register that runs out of paper are harder to place. Emmet (1913) judged that the story "as it stands is full of impossibilities and bombastic exaggerations, but each one of the incidents taken singly may well rest on some basis of fact."
Read as a story of providence

The chapter has no miracle and no angel. God works through the ordinary: a list that cannot be finished, a shortage of paper. The writer names this "providence" (4:21), a Greek word for God's care, and the reader learns to see God's hand where the king sees only clerks' excuses.

views.O: The book's readers in the church were Eastern. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85) count "of the Maccabees, three," and Theodoret summarized this book as history; the Western church did not take it up (Emmet, 1913). Orthodox Bibles print it in the Old Testament (so the list in the Orthodox Study Bible).
views.H: Critical scholars use the register (4:14–21) to date the book: Tcherikover (1945) saw behind it the census taken under Augustus, Emmet (1913) a registration of the Ptolemaic age. Emmet called the chapter's numbers "bombastic exaggerations." The mourning scenes are written in a heightened, rhetorical style.
views.J: No ancient Jewish writing refers to 3 Maccabees (Emmet, 1913; the NETS introduction), so there is no early Jewish reading of it to report. Readers who know Esther will notice a pattern: the decree goes out, the Jews mourn in every place it arrives (Esther 4:3), and the enemy feasts (Esther 3:15). The chapter is the dark half of a pattern that Esther completes with a feast.
views.N: For readers of the New Testament the chapter shows the world of Diaspora Jews whom an official list could ruin. Luke's registration under Augustus (Luke 2:1–3) uses the same Greek word, and 1 Peter's "resident aliens" (1 Peter 1:17) share the Egyptian Jews' sense of living in a land not their own.
views.W: Catholic and Protestant readers, who do not count the book as Scripture, read the chapter as a witness to how Jews of Egypt told their history of suffering, and test its picture of God against the Bible's teaching on providence (Proverbs 21:1; Matthew 10:29–30).

deep.b:
The census of 2:28 was meant to fix the Jews' lower status. In chapter 4 it becomes a death list: every Jew is to be registered "name by name" so that all can be killed in one day (4:14). The writer gives the dates later, from the twenty-fifth of Pachon to the fourth of Epiphi, forty days (6:38).

Tcherikover (1945) saw here the readers' own fear of the census under Augustus, which listed those who paid the poll tax and so threatened the Jews' standing among the Greeks. He even thought the census was the writer's own addition to older stories of persecution. Emmet (1913) answered that the word laographia is "entirely in place in the Ptolemaic age." Either way the readers knew what a list could do, and the writer tells them that God can make even a list fail (4:20–21).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the comedy of the papyrus
deep.b: The book is serious, but this scene is close to a joke: the land of papyrus runs out of papyrus. Claude suggests the writer meant readers in Alexandria, a city of scribes and registers, to laugh. The joke makes a point the book keeps making: the state that seems all-powerful is clumsy and forgetful (5:27, 40), and God's providence does not need to be loud. Readers living under a census could laugh at the clerks without saying anything against the ruler of the day.

echoes: Esther 3:15; Esther 4:3; Esther 8:17; Daniel 5:4; Psalm 115:5–7; Luke 2:1–3; 2:28–29; 6:38

settings.what: The king's order to register every Jew
settings.to: his officials and the scribes of Egypt
settings.when: after the Jews of the countryside are penned in the hippodrome
settings.why: To list every Jew by name so that all could be tortured and killed in one day; inside the story it is the machinery of the decree of 3:25.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt, above all in Alexandria. Emmet (1913) thought it was written mainly for Jews, "to encourage and confirm their faith," but also to be read by outsiders as a defense of the Jews' loyalty to the Ptolemies. The book gives no date. Emmet notes that it cannot be later than the fall of the temple in AD 70, and that its "apparent quotation" of the Greek additions to Daniel (6:6) sets an earliest date. Three dates have been argued.
views: Emmet (1913) dated the book about 100 BC from the official language it shares with Ptolemaic papyri, the greeting formula of its letters and its spelling, and held that laographia fits the Ptolemaic age. Swete reports Thackeray's date: "probably c. 80 B.C."

Tcherikover (1945): the book has in mind an extraordinary census that threatened the Jews' civic status, which fits the census under Augustus that listed those who paid the poll tax; he read the book as written in hatred of Rome.

Ewald (with Hausrath and Reuss, as Swete reports) linked the book to Caligula's attempt to set up his image in the temple and the persecution of the Jews of Alexandria. Emmet answered that the book lacks the marks of that story and that its tone is not that of a time of oppression.

title: Sleep, Forgetting, and the Third Order
sum: The king orders his elephant master Hermon to make five hundred elephants drunk with wine and frankincense and drive them into the Jews the next morning. The Jews, chained in the hippodrome, cry to "the Lord Almighty ... their merciful God and Father." God sends the king a deep sleep, and he sleeps through the hour of the massacre.

Woken late in the afternoon, the king orders the killing for the next day. But at dawn God puts "a forgetting" into his mind: he does not know what Hermon is talking about, praises the Jews' loyalty and threatens Hermon instead. Then, at his banquet, he gives the order a third time and swears to destroy Judea and its temple. At dawn the beasts march out, and the Jews, embracing their children for the last time, fall on their faces and cry to God at the gates of Hades.
readings: The chapter shows God working on the king himself: first his body (sleep), then his mind (forgetting). "God, Master over all, was at work in this" (5:28). The Jews do nothing but pray, and each prayer is followed by a delay.

The king is a figure of fun: he sleeps through his own massacre, forgets his own orders, and flies at his servants for doing what he told them. His Kinsmen tell him so (5:40). The laughter has an edge: a ruler this unstable is dangerous, and the city fills with mobs waiting for plunder (5:41).

views.H: The story outruns history: Ptolemy had seventy-three elephants at Raphia (Polybius 5.79), not five hundred. Josephus's elephant story under Ptolemy Physcon (Against Apion 2.53–55) shows that a story of drunken elephants was told of more than one king; Emmet (1913) thought the writer moved it from Physcon's reign to Philopator's.
views.J: Readers who know Esther can set the chapter beside Esther 6, where sleep flees from the king and the Jews' fortunes turn. In both, God is at work in a king's bedroom without being named by the king.
views.N: For readers of the New Testament the chapter's prayers to God as "Father" (5:7) and its hope for an "appearance" (5:8) are part of the language the first Christians inherited: they would speak of the "appearing" (epiphaneia) of Christ (1 Timothy 6:14; Titus 2:13).
views.W: Western readers, for whom the book is not Scripture, find in it a vivid picture of Jewish trust in God under persecution, while noting that its miracles of sleep and forgetting have no witness outside the story.

deep.b:
The chapter is built on three attempts. (1) The king orders the elephants for the morning (5:2) but God sends sleep (5:11–12). (2) He orders them for the next day (5:20), but God makes him forget (5:27–28). (3) He orders them again and swears an oath (5:38, 42–43), and this time the beasts march (5:46–48). Each time the Jews pray (5:7–9, 13, 25, 50–51), and each time God answers by a larger act, until in chapter 6 he opens heaven.

The writer's word for the working of God in the king is energeia, "working" (5:12, 28), the same word he used of providence in 4:21. The point for readers is that God can rule a hostile ruler from the inside.

deep.h: Elephants in war and in story
deep.b: Hellenistic kings fought with elephants. At Raphia, the battle with which this book begins, Polybius counts seventy-three with Ptolemy and one hundred two with Antiochus III (Polybius 5.79). 1 Maccabees tells how Seleucid soldiers roused their elephants with "the blood of grapes and mulberries" (1 Maccabees 6:34). The writer of 3 Maccabees takes these real weapons and makes them a weapon of execution: five hundred beasts maddened with wine and incense and turned loose on a chained people.

echoes: Esther 6:1; Psalm 127:2; Psalm 121:4; Proverbs 21:1; 1 Maccabees 6:34; Isaiah 38:10; Matthew 16:18

settings.what: The king's first order to Hermon
settings.to: Hermon, the master of the elephants
settings.why: To make the elephants drunk with wine and frankincense and drive them into the Jews the next day.
settings.readers: The order sets out the plan that God will block three times (5:11–12; 5:27–28; 6:18–21).

settings.what: The Jews' cry in the hippodrome
settings.by: the Jews held in the hippodrome
settings.to: God, "the Lord Almighty ... their merciful God and Father"
settings.when: the night before the planned massacre
settings.why: To ask God to overturn the king's plan and rescue them by a visible appearance.
settings.readers: Readers in Alexandria learned from the scene how to pray in danger: not by arms or bribes, but by calling on God together, with tears.

settings.to: Hermon and the guests at his banquet
settings.when: late in the day, after he has slept through the first hour
settings.why: To set the killing again for the next day; inside the story it shows the king's cruelty untouched by his delay.
settings.readers: The readers see the first sign that God is ruling the king's body and mind.

settings.when: at dawn, after God has made him forget his plan
settings.why: Inside the story, the king defends the Jews as his most loyal subjects and threatens Hermon with death in their place.
settings.readers: The readers hear their own claim, that the Jews were the crown's most loyal subjects, from the mouth of their persecutor.

settings.when: at the banquet, after the king has forgotten his plan and then taken it up again
settings.why: To arm the elephants once more for the next day.
settings.readers: Readers see a ruler whose purpose stays cruel even when his memory fails; his own Kinsmen protest (5:40–41).

settings.by: the king's Kinsmen, the highest courtiers
settings.when: at the banquet, after his third order
settings.why: To protest the king's changes of mind and warn that the city is filling with mobs.
settings.readers: For readers the courtiers' complaint mocks a ruler who cannot keep to his own decisions.

settings.why: To bind himself to kill the Jews of Egypt and then march on Judea and burn the temple.
settings.readers: The readers know from chapters 1–2 that the temple has already defeated this king once; the oath, "that could never be carried out," sets up its own failure.

settings.what: The cry at the gates of Hades
settings.by: the Jews, face down in the hippodrome
settings.why: To ask God to show himself and have pity, now that every other hope is gone.
settings.readers: The readers are taught that God hears his people at the last moment, as he did in the past (5:50).

title: Eleazar's Prayer and the Two Angels
sum: As the beasts and the army come on, Eleazar, an old and respected Jew of the countryside, prays for his people. He reminds God how he drowned Pharaoh in the sea, broke Sennacherib, cooled the furnace for the three in Babylonia, brought Daniel up from the lions and kept Jonah alive in the sea monster. If the Jews have sinned in their life abroad, let God punish them himself, not leave them to the idol-worshipers' taunts.

Then God shows his face and opens heaven. Two terrible angels, seen by everyone but the Jews, bind the army with fear, and the elephants turn and trample the king's own troops. The king weeps, turns on his Friends, and frees the Jews as "the sons of the Almighty, heavenly, living God." He provides a seven-day feast in the hippodrome, and the Jews fix these days as a festival for all generations.
readings: The chapter answers the question of every Jewish community abroad: will God, who rescued Israel at the sea and in Babylon, rescue his people here, far from the temple? The answer is yes, in the very place prepared for their death.

The chapter supplies what Hebrew Esther leaves out: an open prayer to God and an open miracle. The ending follows Esther's: a royal reversal, feasting, and a festival made binding for the generations (Esther 9:17–28).

views.H: Emmet (1913) saw in 6:6 "the apparent quotation" of the Greek additions to Daniel and used it to date the book; the prayer also follows the Greek of Leviticus 26:44 (6:15). The angels recall the heavenly riders of 2 Maccabees 3, and the elephant reversal recalls Josephus's story under Ptolemy Physcon (Against Apion 2.53–55). Emmet thought the writer had joined that later story to Philopator's reign; Tcherikover (1945) also read chapters 2:25 to 7 as a story of the later persecution.
views.J: The festival is the chapter's Jewish center. Like Purim it marks a rescue in the Diaspora, by feasting and joy, and it is made binding on the community for all generations (6:36). Josephus knew of a festival of the Alexandrian Jews for a rescue from elephants (Against Apion 2.55). The list of past rescues in the prayer matches the form of the fast-day prayers in Mishnah Ta'anit 2:4.
views.N: For readers of the New Testament the chapter shows the hope of rescue by angels that Acts tells of (Acts 5:19; Acts 12:7), and the list of rescues that Hebrews calls the deeds of faith (Hebrews 11:33–34). Its pagan king calling the Jews God's sons (6:28) looks ahead to Paul's "sons of the living God" (Romans 9:26).
views.W: For Catholic and Protestant churches the book is not Scripture. Readers there can still value Eleazar's prayer as an example of Jewish prayer before Christ, while noting what it adds to the biblical stories: Jonah shown to his people (6:8), and the dew in the furnace (6:6), which comes from the Greek additions to Daniel, Scripture for Catholics but not for Protestants.

deep.h: The prayer and the history of rescue
deep.b:
Eleazar's prayer (6:2–15) has three parts. First he names God (6:2–3): King, Most High, God Almighty, pilot of creation, and the Jews as Abraham's offspring and God's own portion. Then he recalls five rescues (6:4–8): the Exodus, Sennacherib, the furnace, the lions' den, Jonah. Each was from a foreign power or a deadly place, and each fits the Jews' danger: an Egyptian king, a boasting army, death by fire or beasts, a living grave. Last he asks (6:9–15): show yourself now, and if we have sinned, punish us yourself; do not let the Gentiles say our God failed us.

Simon's prayer in Jerusalem (2:2–20) used the same method with the giants, Sodom and Pharaoh. The Mishnah's prayers for fast days still do it centuries later: "He Who answered Abraham on Mount Moriah" will answer us (Mishnah Ta'anit 2:4).

The end of the chapter follows Esther closely. A royal reversal frees the Jews (6:27–29; Esther 8:7–14). There is feasting at royal or public expense (6:30, 40; Esther 8:17; 9:17–19). The days are fixed by the community as days of joy for all generations (6:36; Esther 9:27–28). The feasting lasts "until the fourteenth" (6:40), and the village Jews of Esther keep the fourteenth of Adar (Esther 9:19), though that is a likeness of numbers only, since the months are different.

The differences are real. Esther's feast is fixed by letters of Mordecai and Esther (Esther 9:20–32); here the Jews of Egypt decide it "in common." Esther's dates are Jewish (Adar); these are Egyptian (Pachon and Epiphi, 6:38). And this writer adds a moral note: the days are "not for the sake of drinking and gluttony." Emmet (1913) suggested that the book may have been read aloud at such festivals. Nothing outside the book shows that this festival was kept; Josephus reports a day kept by the Alexandrian Jews for a like rescue from elephants (Against Apion 2.55), but he ties it to another king (see the note on 7:19).

echoes: Exodus 14:28; Exodus 15:11; 2 Kings 19:35; Daniel 3:22–27; Daniel 6:22–23; Jonah 2:10; Leviticus 26:44; Numbers 6:25; Psalm 116:13; Esther 9:17–28; Hebrews 11:33–34

settings.by: Eleazar, an old and respected Jew of the countryside (a priest in Codex Venetus)
settings.to: God, for the Jews held in the hippodrome, with the elders and families around him
settings.when: as the king, the army and the drunken elephants enter the hippodrome
settings.why: To remind God of his past rescues, confess that the people may have sinned, and ask him to act for the sake of his name before the Gentiles; it gathers the cries of the crowd into one voice.
settings.readers: For the Jews of Egypt the prayer taught them to place their own danger inside Israel's history: the God of the Exodus was still the God of Jews in Egypt. On who the book's first readers were and when it was written, see the setting at 4:13–15.

settings.what: The king's speech to his Friends
settings.to: his Friends, the courtiers who had urged the decree
settings.when: after the angels appear and the elephants turn on his army
settings.why: Inside the story, to shift the blame for the decree to his advisers, praise the Jews' loyalty and order their release.
settings.readers: Readers would have recognized the pattern of Greek Esther's Addition E, where the king blames Haman, and heard their own loyalty confirmed by a king.

settings.what: The king's order for the feast
settings.to: the officer in charge of the revenues
settings.when: after the Jews are set free
settings.why: To supply the Jews with wine and food for seven days, so that they celebrate their rescue in the very place set for their death.
settings.readers: The order turns the hippodrome from a place of execution into a place of feasting, and gives readers the royal start of the feast they are told to keep (6:36).

settings.to: their whole community abroad, for all generations
settings.when: during the seven days of feasting in the hippodrome
settings.why: To keep the days of rescue as days of joy, "not for the sake of drinking and gluttony," but in thanks to God.
settings.readers: The rule speaks to readers who may have kept such a festival themselves (compare Josephus, Against Apion 2.55): it gives them the story behind it and the right way to keep it.

settings.what: The Jews' petition to go home
settings.when: at the end of the feasting, on the fourteenth (6:40)
settings.why: To ask leave to return to their homes; the king answers with the letter of 7:1–9.
settings.readers: Emmet (1913) notes that the verb used (entynchanō) is the papyri's technical word for a petition to a king: readers saw the Jews act as loyal subjects who used the proper channels.

title: The Letter, the Renegades, and the Road Home
sum: The king writes to his governors. His Friends, he says, misled him; the Jews are loyal, and the God of heaven fights for them "as a father for his sons." No one may harm or taunt them, for whoever does will have the Most High God as his enemy.

Before going home, the Jews ask the king for leave to punish the Jews who had given up God's law. He grants it, with no trial, and on their way they kill more than three hundred of them, and keep that day as a day of joy. The faithful then travel home, crowned with flowers. At Ptolemais they feast again, fix these days as a festival, set them up on a pillar and found a place of prayer. They return to their homes with great standing among their enemies, and get back all their goods.
readings: Read as the book's happy ending

A royal letter undoes the first letter, the people go home in honor, and a festival keeps the memory. For readers in Egypt this was the hope the book offered: loyalty to God and loyalty to the king need not conflict.

Before the happy ending comes a killing. Jews who had given up the Law are put to death by their own people without trial, and the killing is celebrated. The book approves of it. Honest reading has to face this: the same story that prays against the cruelty of the king ends with its heroes doing a cruelty of their own.

views.H: Emmet (1913) found the letter's opening formula in papyri of about 100 BC and in the Letter of Aristeas; in form and purpose it is close to Addition E of Greek Esther. The killing of the renegades (7:10–15) shows how sharp the line between faithful Jews and those who joined pagan cults was for the writer's community, whatever actually happened.
views.J: The ending sets this festival beside Purim, with a feast, a written record and a yearly keeping (7:19–20). The number three hundred may echo the dead of Susa (Esther 9:15), but there the dead were enemies who attacked the Jews; here they are Jews who left the Law. Biblical law required a careful inquiry and witnesses before anyone was put to death for serving other gods (Deuteronomy 13:14; Deuteronomy 17:4–6), and the book's account has neither.
views.N: For readers of the New Testament the chapter's "time as resident aliens" (7:19) is the phrase of 1 Peter 1:17, and its "place of prayer" (7:20) is the word Luke uses at Philippi (Acts 16:13). The killing of the renegades shows the kind of zeal that Paul once had against the church (Galatians 1:13–14) and that Jesus rebuked in his disciples (Luke 9:54–55).
views.W: Catholic and Protestant churches do not count the book as Scripture. Their readers can take from this chapter a reason for caution: the book teaches trust in God, but it also blesses the killing of fellow Jews who had left the faith, with no trial.

deep.h: Two letters, as in Greek Esther
deep.b: 3 Maccabees and Greek Esther both give the full text of two royal letters: a decree of death (3:12–29; Addition B after Esther 3:13) and a letter of reversal (7:1–9; Addition E after Esther 8:12). In both second letters the king says that evil advisers deceived him, that the Jews are loyal and live by just laws, and that their God protects them; Esther's king calls them "children of the Most High," and Ptolemy says God fights for them "as a father for his sons" (7:6). Hebrew Esther has neither letter. On the two letters of Greek Esther, see the variants at Esther 3:13 and Esther 8:12.

What the text says. The faithful Jews ask the king for leave to punish "those of the Jewish race who had willfully broken faith with the holy God by breaking God's law" (7:10). Their reason is political as well as religious: people who betray God for their stomachs will betray the king too (7:11). The king accepts their reason, "urged them on," and grants it "without needing any royal authority or review" (7:12). They kill more than three hundred on the road and celebrate the day (7:14–15). The writer approves: the dead are "the unholy," and the priests shout "Hallelujah" (7:13).

Within the book. The renegades are most likely those who took the king's offer of citizenship through the mysteries of Dionysus (2:30–33). The book has already shown the faithful shunning them (2:33). The killing completes the line the book draws between faithful Jews, who were nearly killed for their faith, and those who bought safety by giving it up.

Against the Law. The Law did command death for those who led Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6–10), and the zeal of Phinehas and Mattathias is praised (Numbers 25:7–8; 1 Maccabees 2:24–26). But for a man or woman who had served other gods it required that the case be looked into "with care" and proved by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:2–7; compare Deuteronomy 13:14). Here there is no review at all.

Against the Gospel, as this page reads it. Jesus rebuked the disciples who wanted fire on a village that refused him (Luke 9:54–55), and Paul writes, "never take revenge yourselves" (Romans 12:19). Those verses speak of a village and of personal revenge, not directly of this case, so the contrast is this page's reading, not a settled verdict.

deep.title: Claude's reading: the cost of a happy ending
deep.b: Claude suggests the passage is best read as the writer's own limit, not hidden or excused. The book's whole argument is that persecution for faith is wrong and that God defends the faithful; it then ends with its heroes killing for faith, with a king's license and no trial. The writer does not seem to see the irony, but readers can. The book's own prayer to God, "you who hate arrogance, rich in mercy" (6:9), judges this scene better than the writer did. That is also how the Bible itself treats some of its heroes' violence, as in Jacob's verdict on Simeon and Levi (Genesis 49:5–7).

The book says the festival was fixed twice, in Alexandria (6:36) and at Ptolemais (7:19), and written on a pillar (7:20). Nothing outside the book shows that this festival was kept. Josephus tells how drunken elephants turned on the friends of Ptolemy Physcon and says that the Alexandrian Jews "do with good reason celebrate this day" (Against Apion 2.55). Emmet (1913) took the festival in both stories as a sign that some real event lay behind them, but Josephus ties his day to another king and another occasion, so it cannot be shown to be this book's feast.

echoes: Esther 8:12; Esther 9:15; Esther 8:17; Deuteronomy 13:6–14; Deuteronomy 17:2–7; Numbers 25:7–8; 1 Maccabees 2:24–26; Luke 9:54–55; Romans 12:19; Acts 16:13; 1 Peter 1:17; Romans 11:26

settings.by: Ptolemy IV Philopator, as the story presents him
settings.to: the governors and officials of Egypt
settings.when: after the seven days of feasting, when the Jews ask to go home
settings.why: To clear the Jews of every charge, blame the Friends for the decree, order that no one harm or taunt them, and warn that God himself defends them.
settings.readers: Readers in Egypt, who lived by royal grants and feared slander, heard a king declare them loyal and under God's protection; the letter is the counterpart of the first one (3:12–29). On who the book's first readers were and when it was written, see the setting at 4:13–15.

settings.when: after receiving the letter, before they leave
settings.why: To be allowed to punish Jews who had given up the Law, arguing that they would not be loyal to the king either.
settings.readers: The petition shows readers how sharp the line between the faithful and the apostates was for the writer's community; on how to read it, see the chapter page.
views: The book presents the petition as just and its result as a cause for joy (7:13–15).
Read against the Law and the Gospel
The killing without trial conflicts with the inquiry and witnesses the Law required (Deuteronomy 13:14; Deuteronomy 17:4–6); this site also reads it against Jesus' rebuke in Luke 9:54–55.

settings.what: The festival at Ptolemais and the pillar
settings.to: their community, "for all their time as resident aliens"
settings.when: on the journey home, after landing at Ptolemais
settings.why: To keep these days of rescue every year and mark the place with a pillar and a house of prayer.
settings.readers: The readers are given the origin of a festival and of a place of prayer. Josephus's report of an Alexandrian festival for a rescue from elephants (Against Apion 2.55) shows that some such day was kept, though not that it was this one.

settings.when: at the end of the book
settings.why: To end the story as the books of the Psalms end, with a blessing on God and "Amen."
settings.readers: Readers are invited to join the blessing on "the Rescuer of Israel."
